title: Plant Biology
description: How plants feed themselves and reproduce: photosynthesis, transport, responses and the flowering-plant life cycle.
objectives: Explain photosynthesis and its limiting factors
Describe water/mineral uptake and translocation
Trace pollination to germination in flowering plants

topics.title: Photosynthesis
topics.description: The equation that feeds the world, leaf design, and what limits the rate.
objectives: State the equation and leaf adaptations
Explain limiting factors

lessons.title: Leaves as Solar Factories
lessons.description: Chlorophyll, the photosynthesis equation, and how leaves maximise production.
objectives: Write the word and symbol equations for photosynthesis
Explain five leaf adaptations
State the uses of glucose in plants
lessons.introduction: A cassava leaf turns sunlight, air and water into the garri on your table. No factory on Earth matches it — and it runs silently, for free, while cleaning the air.

contents.title: The equation
contents.body: PHOTOSYNTHESIS: carbon dioxide + water → (light energy + chlorophyll) → glucose + oxygen. Symbol: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2. It happens in CHLOROPLASTS: chlorophyll traps light, splitting water (photolysis — releasing the O2 we breathe) and fixing CO2 into glucose via the Calvin cycle. Glucose is then: RESPIRED for energy (plants respire day and night), CONVERTED to STARCH for storage (tubers, seeds), built into CELLULOSE for walls, combined with nitrates into AMINO ACIDS/PROTEINS, or stored as OILS (palm fruit, groundnut). Without photosynthesis there is no food chain, no oxygen atmosphere, no fossil fuel — every meal and every breath begins here.

contents.title: Leaf adaptations
contents.body: Leaves are optimised on five fronts. (1) BROAD and THIN: huge area catches light; short diffusion paths move gases fast. (2) CHLOROPHYLL packed in palisade mesophyll near the upper surface — most light meets most pigment. (3) STOMATA (pores, mostly underneath) + AIR SPACES let CO2 diffuse in and O2 out; guard cells open/close them to balance gas entry against water loss. (4) VEINS (xylem + phloem) deliver water and export sugars while stiffening the blade. (5) WAXY CUTICLE cuts evaporation while staying transparent. Desert plants modify the plan (spines, sunken stomata, CAM night-photosynthesis); water plants float stomata on top. Examination pattern: adaptation → feature → benefit ('stomata allow CO2 entry for photosynthesis').

contents.title: Worked example: why destarch?
contents.body: Question: Before testing whether light is needed for photosynthesis, a plant is kept in darkness for 48 hours. Why? Step 1 — Recall: leaves STORE starch from earlier photosynthesis. Step 2 — Reason: old starch would give false positives everywhere — you could not tell NEW starch (made in your experiment) from OLD. Step 3 — Conclude: destarching empties the stores so any starch found later MUST have been made during the test — a control against prior conditions. Then the foil-star test (Module 8's final-exam question) proves light's necessity cleanly. Controls separate real causes from leftovers — the mark of valid experiments.

contents.title: Watch: Photosynthesis (UPDATED)
contents.body: Watch 'Photosynthesis (UPDATED)' by the Amoeba Sisters (official channel stream). Sketch and label a leaf cross-section from memory afterwards.

contents.title: Key concepts
contents.body:
6CO2 + 6H2O →(light/chlorophyll) C6H12O6 + 6O2 in chloroplasts.
Glucose fates: respire, starch, cellulose, protein (with nitrates), oils.
Leaf wins: broad, chlorophyll-rich, stomata + air spaces, veins, cuticle.
Destarch before starch tests — controls rule out old stores.

contents.title: Lesson summary
contents.body: Leaves are solar factories tuned by five adaptations, running the equation that feeds and oxygenates the planet. Glucose then branches into energy, stores, walls and proteins.

lessons.title: Limiting Factors
lessons.description: Light, CO2 and temperature — which factor caps the rate, and how farmers exploit the answer.
objectives: Define limiting factor
Interpret rate graphs for light, CO2 and temperature
Explain two greenhouse techniques that raise yield
lessons.introduction: A greenhouse farmer pumps in extra CO2 and harvests 30% more tomatoes. Same seeds, same soil — just one bottleneck removed. Limiting factors are profit.

contents.title: Three graphs, one idea
contents.body: A LIMITING FACTOR is the variable holding back the rate — raising it (alone) raises the rate until something else limits. LIGHT INTENSITY: rate climbs then plateaus (light no longer limits — CO2 or temperature does). CARBON DIOXIDE: same shape — enrichment boosts glasshouse crops until light/temperature cap out (note: open-field CO2 (~0.04%) almost always limits). TEMPERATURE: rises to an optimum (~25–35°C for most crops) then FALLS as enzymes denature — the asymmetric enzyme curve from Module 3. WATER rarely limits rate directly (except drought closing stomata). Measuring rate: oxygen bubbles from pondweed per minute, or CO2 uptake via sensors — with temperature, light and CO2 controlled except the one under test.

contents.title: Worked example: reading the plateau
contents.body: Question: A farmer doubles lamp brightness over lettuce but yield does not rise. CO2 is at outdoor levels, temperature 20°C. Advise her. Step 1 — Diagnose: the light curve has PLATEAUED — light no longer limits; CO2 (or temperature) does. Step 2 — Prescribe: enrich CO2 (burners, fermentation tanks, or simply ventilate less) and/or warm toward the optimum — THEN extra light pays. Step 3 — Generalise: always find the CURRENT bottleneck before spending on inputs — fertiliser cannot fix a light shortage, water cannot fix nitrogen lack. This is Liebig's Law of the Minimum: growth is capped by the scarcest resource.

contents.title: Key concepts
contents.body:
Limiting factor = the variable currently capping the rate.
Light and CO2 give rise-then-plateau; temperature gives optimum-then-denaturation fall.
Greenhouses enrich CO2, warm air and extend light — removing bottlenecks in order.
Liebig's Law: the scarcest resource sets the ceiling.

contents.title: Lesson summary
contents.body: Photosynthesis obeys bottlenecks: light, CO2 and temperature each cap the rate in turn. Read the curve, find the ceiling, lift it — the logic behind greenhouses and fertiliser advice alike.

topics.title: Transport and Responses
topics.description: Xylem and phloem, transpiration pull, and how plants sense light and gravity.
objectives: Contrast xylem and phloem
Explain transpiration stream and tropisms

lessons.title: Moving Water and Food
lessons.description: Root uptake, the transpiration stream, and translocation of sugars.
objectives: Trace water from soil to leaf
Explain how transpiration pulls the stream
State what phloem translocates and between which organs
lessons.introduction: A 30-metre iroko lifts hundreds of litres daily with no pump, no heart, no energy bill. It runs on evaporation — physics as plumbing.

contents.title: Xylem: the water lift
contents.body: ROOT HAIRS absorb soil water by OSMOSIS (Module 2) and minerals by ACTIVE TRANSPORT — their millions of extensions multiply area. Water crosses the root cortex to the XYLEM: dead, hollow, lignin-strengthened tubes running root → stem → leaf. The TRANSPIRATION STREAM pulls it up: (1) leaf cells lose water vapour through stomata (TRANSPIRATION — driven by heat, wind, dry air); (2) lost water is replaced from xylem; (3) water's COHESION (molecules gripping each other) + ADHESION (gripping walls) drags the whole column upward — one unbroken rope from roots to crown. Stomata regulate the trade: open for CO2 (photosynthesis) but losing water; closing in drought (abscisic acid triggers it) saves water but starves CO2. Wilting is lost turgor when loss beats uptake — recovered by watering, not by magic.

contents.title: Phloem: the food network
contents.body: PHLOEM (sieve tubes + companion cells — living, no nuclei in sieve elements) TRANSLOCATES sugars and amino acids from SOURCES (photosynthesising leaves, or storage organs in spring) to SINKS (roots, fruits, growing tips, storage tubers) — in ANY direction, unlike xylem's one-way climb. Flow is driven by pressure gradients (mass flow): sources load sugar (water follows by osmosis, raising pressure), sinks unload it (pressure falls) — sap streams from high to low pressure. Farmers exploit both systems: ring-barking (removing phloem) swells fruits above the cut; grafting joins one plant's shoot to another's roots via aligned cambia. Mineral needs: nitrates (proteins — deficiency yellows old leaves first), phosphates (roots/DNA/ATP), potassium (enzymes/stomata), magnesium (chlorophyll — deficiency yellows between veins).

contents.title: Worked example: the bagged branch
contents.body: Question: A clear plastic bag tied over a leafy branch collects water droplets inside by evening; a bag over a leafless branch stays dry. Explain. Step 1 — Source: droplets condensed from vapour the LEAVES transpired (stomata → air → bag → cool plastic → condense). Step 2 — Control: the leafless bag proves leaves (not bark or air) are the water source. Step 3 — Conclude: visible proof of transpiration — and your module practical repeats exactly this. Extension: morning vs noon bags show the rate follows heat/light — transpiration's drivers made visible.

contents.title: Key concepts
contents.body:
Root hairs (osmosis + active transport) → xylem (dead tubes) → transpiration pull (cohesion) → leaf.
Stomata trade CO2 entry against water loss.
Phloem translocates sugars source → sink in any direction.
Deficiency clues: yellow old leaves (nitrate), yellow between veins (magnesium).

contents.title: Lesson summary
contents.body: Xylem lifts by evaporation-pull through dead pipes; phloem delivers by pressure-flow through living ones. Stomata govern the water-carbon trade, and mineral shortages write their symptoms on leaves.

lessons.title: How Plants Respond
lessons.description: Tropisms and hormones: auxin steering growth toward light and with gravity.
objectives: Define phototropism and gravitropism (geotropism)
Explain auxin's role in bending
Give two agricultural uses of plant hormones
lessons.introduction: A seedling on your windowsill bends toward the light within days — with no eyes, muscles or brain. Hormones do the steering.

contents.title: Auxin steering
contents.body: TROPISM = directional growth response: PHOTOTROPISM (to light — shoots bend toward it) and GRAVITROPISM/GEOTROPISM (to gravity — roots grow down/positive, shoots grow up/negative). The hormone AUXIN (made in shoot tips) drives it: light makes auxin accumulate on the SHADED side; in SHOOTS, extra auxin SPEEDS cell elongation there — the shaded side outgrows the lit side, bending the shoot TOWARD light. In ROOTS the same extra auxin SLOWS elongation — the lower side grows less, bending the root DOWNWARD. One hormone, opposite effects by tissue — an examination favourite. Other hormones: GIBBERELLINS (stem elongation, seed germination — brewers sprout barley with them), CYTOKININS (cell division), ABSCISIC ACID (drought response — closes stomata, drops leaves), ETHENE (fruit ripening — traders ripen plantain with it).

contents.title: Worked example: the dark box
contents.body: Question: Two identical seedlings: A in a box with a side hole (light one-sided), B in a fully dark box. After 5 days A bends toward the hole; B grows tall, pale and straight. Explain both. Step 1 — A: one-sided light → auxin gathers on the shaded side → faster elongation there → bends TOWARD light (positive phototropism). Step 2 — B: no light → auxin spreads evenly → straight growth; paleness = no chlorophyll made (etiolation) and tallness = the seedling 'searching' for light. Step 3 — Conclude: light DIRECTION steers (A), light ABSENCE starves (B) — tropism needs a gradient, which darkness cannot provide.

contents.title: Key concepts
contents.body:
Shoots: positive phototropism, negative gravitropism. Roots: positive gravitropism.
Auxin gathers shaded/lower; speeds shoots, slows roots — bending both correctly.
Gibberellins germinate, ethene ripens, abscisic acid drought-proofs.
Tropisms need gradients; uniform conditions give straight growth.

contents.title: Lesson summary
contents.body: Plants navigate with hormones: auxin gradients bend shoots to light and roots to earth. Farmers hijack the same signals to germinate, ripen and root crops on schedule.

topics.title: Reproduction in Flowering Plants
topics.description: Flower structure, pollination, fertilisation, seeds and germination.
objectives: Label flower parts
Trace pollination to germination

lessons.title: Flowers and Pollination
lessons.description: Male and female parts, insect vs wind strategies, and fertilisation's double event.
objectives: Label sepals, petals, stamens, carpels and their sub-parts
Contrast insect- and wind-pollinated flowers with four features each
Describe the pollen tube journey to the ovule
lessons.introduction: A flower is advertising, engineering and nursery in one: colours and scents bribe couriers, structures load and receive pollen, and ovaries become the fruits we eat.

contents.title: Structure and strategies
contents.body: Flower parts: SEPALS (green, protect the bud) → PETALS (often bright/scented, attract insects) → STAMENS (male: anther makes POLLEN, filament holds it) → CARPEL(s) (female: stigma catches pollen, style connects, ovary holds OVULES with egg cells). INSECT-pollinated flowers: large bright petals, scent, nectar guides, sticky/spiky pollen, sticky stigma. WIND-pollinated (maize, grasses): tiny dull petals, NO scent/nectar, HUGE pollen quantities, light smooth grains, large FEATHERY stigmas dangling to catch drifting pollen, anthers dangling outside. POLLINATION = pollen landing on stigma (self: same flower/plant — fast, no variation; cross: different plant — variation, needs couriers). FERTILISATION follows: pollen germinates, a tube grows down the style, male nuclei enter the ovule — one fuses with the EGG (zygote → embryo), one fuses with endosperm nuclei (food store) — flowering plants' unique DOUBLE fertilisation.

contents.title: Worked example: maize tassels
contents.body: Question: Maize grows male tassels at the very top and female silks (stigmas) lower down. Explain how this arrangement suits wind pollination AND reduces self-pollination. Step 1 — Wind logic: top tassels release clouds of light pollen that drift DOWN onto the feathery silks below — gravity assists the wind. Step 2 — Outbreeding logic: tassels shed pollen BEFORE most local silks emerge (or wind carries it to neighbouring plants first), favouring CROSS-pollination and variation. Step 3 — Conclude: position + timing turn wind from a gamble into a system — engineering without engineers. (Farmers bag tassels/silks to force controlled crosses in breeding programmes.)

contents.title: Key concepts
contents.body:
Stamen = anther + filament (male). Carpel = stigma + style + ovary (female).
Insect: showy, scented, sticky. Wind: dull, huge pollen, feathery stigmas.
Pollination (transfer) precedes fertilisation (fusion) — never swap the terms.
Double fertilisation: zygote + endosperm food store.

contents.title: Lesson summary
contents.body: Flowers match their couriers: insect flowers advertise, wind flowers mass-produce. Pollen's landing is pollination; the tube's delivery is fertilisation — and the ovary's reward is fruit.

lessons.title: Seeds and Germination
lessons.description: How fruits spread seeds, what seeds contain, and the three conditions for sprouting.
objectives: Explain four seed-dispersal mechanisms with examples
Label a seed (testa, embryo, food store)
State germination requirements and how to test each
lessons.introduction: A mango seed cannot walk to a new clearing — so the fruit bribes you to carry it. Dispersal is the plant kingdom's travel industry.

contents.title: Dispersal and the seed
contents.body: After fertilisation, the OVARY wall becomes the FRUIT and OVULES become SEEDS (embryo + food store + protective TESTA). Dispersal methods: WIND — light, winged/plumed seeds (Tridax daisy fluff, mahogany wings); ANIMALS — tasty fruits eaten and dropped (mango, guava) or hooked burrs hitching fur/clothes (grasses); WATER — floating fibrous fruits (coconut husks ride oceans); EXPLOSIVE — pods flinging seeds (oil bean/pentaclethra, peas). Seeds contain the EMBRYO (plumule → shoot, radicle → root) plus food (endosperm or fat cotyledons — beans' fleshy halves). GERMINATION needs three conditions: WATER (activates enzymes, softens testa), OXYGEN (aerobic respiration for growth energy), and WARMTH (enzyme optimum) — light is NOT required (most seeds germinate underground; its absence even helps some).

contents.title: Worked example: testing germination needs
contents.body: Question: Design a test of whether water is needed for germination. Step 1 — Setup: two petri dishes (or plates with cotton wool), 10 bean seeds each, same warmth and air. DISH A: cotton wool DAMP. DISH B: cotton wool DRY (seeds present, everything else identical). Step 2 — Observe 5 days: A sprouts (radicles emerge), B stays hard. Step 3 — Conclude: water is necessary — the ONLY difference was water, so it caused the difference. Fair-test checklist: same seed type/number, same temperature, same air, only water varied. Repeat-logic gives the oxygen test (boiled-cooled water + oil layer excludes air) and warmth test (fridge vs room).

contents.title: Key concepts
contents.body:
Fruit = ripened ovary; seed = embryo + store + testa. Dispersal: wind, animal, water, explosive.
Germination needs water + oxygen + warmth — NOT light.
Test one condition at a time; everything else identical.
Radicle (root) emerges first, then plumule (shoot).

contents.title: Lesson summary
contents.body: Fruits are travel agents, seeds are packed lunches with babies inside, and germination waits only for water, air and warmth. Test each requirement by varying one factor — fair tests again.

practical.title: Starch in Leaves + Transpiration Bags
practical.objective: Prove photosynthesis makes starch and make transpiration visible.
practical.scenario: Two classic experiments, one afternoon — a destarched plant and a leafy branch.
practical.instructions: PART A — STARCH TEST: 1. Destarch: keep a potted plant (or one branch covered) in darkness 48 hours. 2. Cover part of one leaf with foil (a shape), expose the plant to bright light 6+ hours. 3. Pluck the leaf: boil 2 min in water (soften, kill), then boil in ethanol in a HOT WATER BATH (no open flame — ethanol burns!) until pale, rinse, then add iodine. 4. Record: which areas turn blue-black? PART B — TRANSPIRATION: 5. Tie a clear dry bag over a leafy branch and another over a bare twig; leave 3 hours in sun. 6. Compare droplets. SAFETY: adult supervision for boiling; ethanol ONLY in a water bath away from flames; iodine stains; wash hands.
practical.requirements: Potted plant, foil, ethanol, iodine, water bath/kettle, 2 clear bags, string.
practical.expected_output: Starch-test sketch with labelled areas + bag comparison + two conclusions (light→starch; leaves transpire).
evaluation_criteria: Ethanol safety step stated and followed
Both conclusions link evidence to photosynthesis/transpiration

assignment.title: Design a School Garden
assignment.description: Plan a productive 5 m × 5 m school garden applying photosynthesis, transport, soils and reproduction science.
assignment.instructions: Your school grants a 5 m × 5 m plot. Submit: (1) CROPS: choose 4 crops (one legume compulsory — explain its nitrogen gift) with spacing and reasons (light needs, root depth, season). (2) LAYOUT: describe/draw (in words) bed positions — tall crops north/south? paths? compost corner? water source? Justify with light/shade and labour logic. (3) CALENDAR: month-by-month for one term — sowing, weeding, watering, harvest. (4) SCIENCE NOTES: 200 words linking THREE module concepts to your choices (e.g. limiting factors → spacing; transpiration → mulching; pollination → border flowers for bees). (5) BUDGET: rough costs (seeds, tools, water) under a sensible total. 500–600 words total.
assignment.requirements: Must suit a real Nigerian school season and budget; fantasy tractors score zero.
assignment.expected_output: Crop plan + layout + calendar + science notes + budget (500–600 words).
evaluation_criteria: Legume included with correct nitrogen-fixation reasoning
Three module concepts applied correctly to real choices

quiz.title: Module 9 Quiz — Plant Biology
quiz.description: Quick check on photosynthesis, transport and reproduction.

questions.question: The correct photosynthesis equation is:
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis builds glucose from CO2 + water using light (oxygen released). The second equation is respiration — the reverse.

questions.question: Plants are destarched before photosynthesis experiments to:
options: Remove old starch so only newly made starch is detected
questions.explanation: Old stores would false-positive every test. Destarching ensures detected starch was made DURING the experiment.

questions.question: Water rises in xylem mainly by:
options: Transpiration pull via cohesion of water molecules
questions.explanation: Evaporation from leaves drags the cohesive water column up dead xylem tubes. Root pressure helps only short distances.

questions.question: Shoots bend toward light because auxin:
options: Gathers on the lit side and stops all growth
Gathers on the shaded side, speeding elongation there
questions.explanation: Uneven auxin → uneven growth → bending toward light. (In roots the same extra auxin slows growth, bending them down.)

questions.question: Germination of most seeds requires:
questions.explanation: Water activates enzymes, oxygen fuels respiration, warmth optimises it. Light is NOT needed (seeds sprout underground).

assessment.title: Module 9 Examination — Plant Biology
assessment.description: End-of-module examination covering photosynthesis, transport, responses and reproduction.
assessment.instructions: Answer ALL 6 questions in 25 minutes. Pass mark is 60%. Counts toward your final assessment gate.

questions.question: Raising light intensity stops increasing photosynthesis rate at high levels because:
options: Another factor (CO2 or temperature) becomes limiting
questions.explanation: Plateaus mean the raised factor no longer limits — the ceiling moved to CO2 supply or temperature/enzyme capacity.

questions.question: Phloem translocates sugars:
options: From sources to sinks in any direction
questions.explanation: Pressure-driven mass flow follows source→sink gradients: leaves→roots in summer, stores→buds in spring — any direction needed.

questions.question: Wind-pollinated flowers typically have:
options: Small dull petals, huge light pollen, feathery stigmas
questions.explanation: Wind flowers mass-produce cheap pollen and maximise capture area — no advertising budget needed.

questions.question: True or False: Double fertilisation in flowering plants produces both the zygote and the endosperm food store.
questions.explanation: True. One male nucleus fuses the egg (embryo), the second fuses endosperm nuclei (food) — unique to flowering plants.

questions.question: Old leaves yellowing first (chlorosis from the bottom up) most likely indicates deficiency of:
options: A mobile nutrient like nitrogen — the plant salvages it to young leaves
questions.explanation: Mobile nutrients (N, P, K, Mg) are withdrawn from old leaves to growing tips — so old leaves yellow first. Immobile deficiencies (Fe, Ca) strike young leaves.

questions.question: Which are leaf adaptations for photosynthesis? (Select ALL that apply)
options: Broad thin shape with large surface area
Chlorophyll-rich palisade layer near the top
Stomata and air spaces for gas diffusion
Thick opaque hairs blocking all light
questions.explanation: Area, pigment placement and gas routes all boost photosynthesis. Blocking light would sabotage it (hairs reduce water loss, not boost photosynthesis).
